episodes.162583: A warm front moved northward into southwest Missouri during the early morning of the 23rd and set up a boundary for training showers and thunderstorms from southeast Kansas eastward into south central Missouri. The heaviest rainfall occurred from Crawford County, Kansas to Lawrence County, Missouri,  where accumulations exceeded three inches.
episodes.162959: An isolated strong thunderstorm developed along a cold front in north Georgia.
episodes.163032: An atmospheric river aided in heavy rain development across the River Complex burn scar. One or possibly more debris flows occurred as a result. Removal, protective measures, and repair costs from this debris flow are estimated to be $3.2 million.
episodes.163089: A line of showers and thunderstorms ahead of an approaching cold front pushed into the western highlands of Pennsylvania during the evening of October 21, 2021. A couple of the storms in this line produced wind damage, including a microburst near Horseshoe Curve in western Blair County.
episodes.163156: Several rounds of heavy rain occurred across northwest California from October 21st to October 25th. The first round of heavy rainfall was associated with a frontal passage, and that event yielded rainfall rates sufficient for debris flows occurring across the River Complex burn scar. The next heavy rainfall event was associated with a classic atmospheric river on October 24th. Impacts were mainly limited to nuisance flooding.
episodes.163539: A strong atmospheric river event produced a major heavy rain, high wind, and high elevation snow event for much of the region. Record-setting rainfall amounts for many areas of the Sierra into western Nevada. NWS Reno received multiple reports of mud and rock slides in the Sierra along I-80 near the summit, and CA 70 and CA 89 in Sierra, Plumas, and Lassen Counties.
episodes.163588: A broken line of supercells, which formed along a front, moved quickly through the Ohio River Valley the evening of October 21st and spun off several tornadoes. The number of tornadoes, time of year, and intensity (one long track EF2 tornado) will mark this event as very rare and significant for this region. ||Prior to tornado development, surface temperatures warmed into the low-mid 60s; dew points topped out near 60F.  Forecast soundings indicated modest levels of mean layer CAPE, and a relatively straight hodograph yielding marginal but sufficient storm relative helicity. The overall quick track of the broken line and eastward propagation helped cells sustain rotating updrafts.
episodes.163598: An upper level disturbance moved northward from Mexico and provided lift over West Texas. Low-level moisture had increased across the area which contributed to higher instability. Wind shear was also fairly high across the area. The instability was hindered somewhat by cloud cover but was enough for storms to develop and move through Brewster County. These storms produced a flash flood and a severe wind gust.
episodes.163780: An influx of deep moisture across South Florida interacting with a low pressure trough over the Florida peninsula led to the development of heavy showers and thunderstorms across the region.
episodes.163782: An influx of deep moisture across South Florida interacting with a low pressure trough over the Florida peninsula led to the development of heavy showers and thunderstorms across the region.
episodes.163982: An upper-level disturbance interacted with the sea-breeze to help ignite a few thunderstorms across the Lower Rio Grande Valley on October 22nd. A downburst from one of these storms produced strong wind gusts in western Harlingen, TX.

events.narrative: A NWS damage survey confirmed that an EF-1 tornado, with winds|speeds ranging between 90 to 95 MPH, tracked through portions of|Peters Township in Washington County on the evening of October|21, 2021. The length was 1.5 miles and the width in some areas|was about 100 to 200 yards. This tornado was associated with the same |circulation that initially produced an EF-1 tornado in Jefferson |County, OH and an EF-2 in Hopewell Township a few miles to the |west. ||A few broken branches were noted along Thomas Road near|Peters Lake Park. However, the tornado quickly intensified as it|cross Hill Place Road. Trees were uprooted and snapped in the|vicinity of Springdale Road and Sunrise Lane. A number of new and|well-structured brick homes had window damage, a garage blown|out, shingle damage, and trees snapped. The tornado weakened and|dissipated just west of Bower Hill Road.||A detailed review by PEMA noted damage to 4 homes on Hill Place Road, |5 homes on Sunrise Road, 5 homes on Springdale Road, 1 home on |Buckingham Drive, and 2 homes on Sienna Trail. |||Damage cost was estimated by NWS Storm Surveyor.
The Gordon County 911 center reported a tree blown down near the intersection of Pine Chapel Road and Red Bud Road.
A thunderstorm moved across Brewster County and produced a 67 mph wind gust in Castolon.
A severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 60 mph knocked down trees and wires in Susquehanna Township.

Heavy rain resulted in flash flooding in Big Bend National Park near Rio Grande Village. Several dirt roads were reported closed or impassible due to debris and mud remaining from localized flash flooding. The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.
A severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 60 mph knocked down a tree at the intersection of Red Schoolhouse Road and Rose Lane to the west of Ashland.

A severe thunderstorm produced a microburst with winds estimated by a NWS Storm Survey to have been between 80 and 90 mph just to the east of Lake Altoona. Trees were snapped and uprooted in a relatively small area near Lakeside Drive.
A severe thunderstorm producing winds estimated near 60 mph knocked down trees and wires west of Altoona.
Minor flooding reported due to heavy rain.

An atmospheric river aided in heavy rain development across the River Complex burn scar. One or possibly more debris flows occurred as a result. Removal, protective measures, and repair costs from this debris flow are estimated to be $3.2 million.
A 24 hour rainfall measurement of 2.24 inches was reported with rain still falling.

Reports received from broadcast media via Twitter of flooding in Fort Lauderdale. One area was at NE 7 Place and NE 20 Avenue where water was almost 1 foot deep along the street and water flowed into the front yards of adjacent homes. The other area was along A1A and Sunrise Boulevard where water covered the roadway but vehicles were still able to get through. |||Nearby rain gauges measured almost 3 inches of rain, most of which fell in just 1 hour.

Pictures received via social media of flooding in the on-ramp from Biscayne Boulevard to I-395 in Downtown Miami. Water covered the roadway but vehicles were still getting through. Rainfall amounts from nearby rain gauges were near 2 inches.

COOP and CoCoRahs observers, as well as Mesonet/ASOS sites, reported rainfall amounts ranging from 1.0-3.0 around Walker, CA, to the Lee Vining/Mono Lake area with 4.0-6.0 around the Crestview to Mammouth Lakes, CA region.

CoCoRahs Observers, trained spotters, and Mesonet/ASOS sites reported rainfall amounts ranging from 0.5-3.0 in the area between Janesville to Susanville, CA; 3.0-4.0 in the Westwood to Lake Almanor region; and up to 6.0 about 3.0 mi SSW of Susanville, CA.||Trained spotter in Doyle at an elevation of 4500 feet reported 7.28 inches of rain as of midnight (24 hour period starting 24/0001 LST) with an additional 1.49 inches falling since midnight.  The spotter also reported that snow was falling around midnight but not accumulating. Total rainfall amount of 8.77 was reported at this site.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 39 knots (45 mph) was recorded by the WxFlow station XDIN on Biscayne Bay.

Thunderstorm winds estimated at 50 knots downed several large tree limbs and felled at least one large mesquite when its base snapped, ripped 3 to 4 pieces of roofing off of a carport on Hoy Street, and lofted a trampoline into powerlines. Damage value is estimated.||Note: The estimated wind gust of 50 knots is equivalent to 58 mph.

Pictures and videos received via Twitter of street flooding in the Mid Beach section of Miami Beach, mainly along Collins Avenue in the area of 29th Street. Water was over curbs and sidewalks with partial lane closures. Rainfall estimates in the area were around 3-4 inches, with much of this likely falling in about 1 hour during the time of the flooding.
